meta.name: Medical tests
meta.about: Medical tests: what each measures, why it is ordered, how it is done, how results are read and what a test cannot tell you. Panels are broken down into their components, each linked to the biomarker it measures. Reference ranges belong to the laboratory that ran the test; guideline thresholds are quoted with their source and country. Written for education, not for interpreting an individual's results.

complete-blood-count.name: Full blood count
complete-blood-count.what: The most commonly ordered blood test: an automated count of the red cells, white cells and platelets in a small sample, with the size and haemoglobin content of the red cells.

measures.meaning: The oxygen-carrying protein; low = anaemia, high = polycythaemia.
Small cells point to iron deficiency, large cells to B12 or folate deficiency or alcohol.
Neutrophils rise with bacterial infection and steroids, lymphocytes with viral infection, eosinophils with allergy and parasites.
Clotting cells; low counts bleed, very high counts may clot or signal inflammation.

whyOrdered: Tiredness, pallor or breathlessness (anaemia)
Suspected infection or inflammation
Unexplained bruising or bleeding
Monitoring chemotherapy and many long-term drugs
Routine pre-operative check
complete-blood-count.how: A few millilitres of blood from an arm vein into a tube with an anticoagulant; results within hours.

interpretation.finding: Low haemoglobin with small red cells
interpretation.meaning: Iron deficiency, usually from blood loss (gut, periods) or poor intake
Bacterial infection, inflammation, steroids or stress
Immune destruction, marrow problems, liver disease, some drugs
Bone marrow failure or infiltration, needs urgent specialist review

complete-blood-count.limitations: Tells you that something is wrong, not what: an abnormal count is a prompt for further tests such as iron studies, a blood film or marrow examination.
complete-blood-count.specimen: Venous blood in an EDTA (anticoagulant) tube
complete-blood-count.resultType: A panel of numeric results, each with its own laboratory reference interval, plus flags for the differential

quick.usedFor: General health, anaemia, infection, blood disorders, monitoring
quick.measures: Blood cells and related indices: red cells, white cells and platelets

components.name: Haemoglobin
components.measures: Oxygen-carrying protein concentration
components.high: Polycythaemia, dehydration, chronic hypoxia, smoking
components.low: Anaemia of any cause: iron, B12 or folate deficiency, blood loss, chronic disease, marrow failure

components.name: Haematocrit
components.measures: Fraction of blood volume occupied by red cells
components.high: Dehydration, polycythaemia

components.name: Red cell count
components.measures: Number of red cells per litre
components.high: Polycythaemia, thalassaemia trait (high count with small cells)

components.name: Mean corpuscular volume
components.measures: Average red-cell size
components.high: B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, some drugs

components.name: Mean corpuscular haemoglobin
components.measures: Average haemoglobin per red cell
components.high: Macrocytosis

components.name: Mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration
components.measures: Haemoglobin concentration within red cells
components.high: Hereditary spherocytosis, dehydration

components.name: Red cell distribution width
components.measures: Variation in red-cell size
components.high: Mixed deficiencies, early iron deficiency, recent transfusion

components.name: White cell count
components.measures: Total leucocytes
components.high: Infection, inflammation, steroids, leukaemia, smoking
components.low: Viral infection, chemotherapy, marrow failure, some drugs

components.name: Neutrophils
components.measures: Cells that fight bacteria (from the differential)
components.high: Bacterial infection, inflammation, steroids, tissue injury
components.low: Chemotherapy, some drugs, viral infection, sepsis, benign ethnic neutropenia

components.name: Lymphocytes
components.measures: Cells of adaptive immunity
components.high: Viral infections, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia

components.name: Monocytes, eosinophils, basophils
components.measures: Other white-cell types in the differential
components.high: Chronic infection (monocytes); allergy, asthma, parasites, drug reactions (eosinophils); myeloproliferative disease (basophils)

components.name: Platelets
components.measures: Clotting cell fragments
components.high: Reactive (infection, inflammation, iron deficiency, bleeding), essential thrombocythaemia
components.low: Immune destruction, drugs, liver disease, marrow failure, sepsis, clumping in the tube

components.name: Mean platelet volume
components.measures: Average platelet size
components.high: Increased platelet turnover

complete-blood-count.rangeNote: Every component has a reference interval that depends on the analyser, age, sex, pregnancy and ethnic background; children's values differ markedly from adults'. The report flags values outside the laboratory's own interval, and a flagged value is a prompt for interpretation, not a diagnosis.
factors: Pregnancy, dehydration and altitude change red-cell values
Recent infection, exercise, smoking, stress and steroids change white cells
Clumping, clotting or delay in the tube gives spurious platelet and cell counts
Ethnic background (benign ethnic neutropenia)
Recent transfusion, iron infusion or bleeding
cannotTell: The cause of an abnormal count: it shows that something has changed, and further tests (iron studies, B12 and folate, a blood film, sometimes marrow examination) show why
Whether platelets are working properly (only their number)
Whether a normal count excludes disease that has not yet affected the blood
complete-blood-count.medicinesNote: Chemotherapy, methotrexate, carbimazole, clozapine and many other medicines lower counts; corticosteroids raise neutrophils and lower lymphocytes and eosinophils; heparin can lower platelets.

blood-glucose.name: Blood glucose
blood-glucose.what: The concentration of glucose in blood, measured from a vein or a fingerprick. Fasting, random and after-a-sugar-drink (oral glucose tolerance) versions answer different questions.

measures.meaning: After 8 hours without food; normal below 5.6 mmol/L, diabetes at 7.0 or above on two occasions.
Any time of day; 11.1 mmol/L or above with symptoms suggests diabetes.
Glucose two hours after a 75 g drink; used in pregnancy and borderline cases.

whyOrdered: Thirst, passing lots of urine, weight loss
Screening for diabetes in people at risk
Confusion, sweating or collapse (hypoglycaemia)
Monitoring insulin and other diabetes treatment
blood-glucose.how: Venous sample in a fluoride tube, or a capillary fingerprick on a meter; continuous glucose monitors sample fluid under the skin.
blood-glucose.preparation: Fasting tests need 8-12 hours without food, water allowed.

interpretation.meaning: Impaired fasting glucose: prediabetes, a chance to change course
Diabetes if repeated or with symptoms
Hypoglycaemia: usually insulin or sulfonylurea excess; treat with fast sugar

blood-glucose.limitations: A single value is a snapshot; HbA1c gives the three-month average. Stress and illness raise glucose temporarily.

references.title: NHS: Type 2 diabetes – symptoms and diagnosis

hba1c.name: HbA1c
hba1c.what: The fraction of haemoglobin that has glucose stuck to it. Because red cells live about 120 days, it reports the average blood glucose over the previous two to three months in a single number.

measures.meaning: Reported in mmol/mol (and %). Below 42 (6.0%) normal; 42-47 (6.0-6.4%) prediabetes; 48 (6.5%) or above diabetes.

whyOrdered: Diagnosing type 2 diabetes
Monitoring diabetes control every 3-6 months
Setting and reviewing treatment targets

interpretation.meaning: Diabetes (if no condition affecting red cells)
Individualised: tighter in the young and newly diagnosed, looser in the frail
Treatment and lifestyle changes are working

hba1c.limitations: Unreliable when red cell life is abnormal: anaemia, haemoglobin variants, recent transfusion, pregnancy, kidney failure. Not for diagnosing type 1 diabetes, which moves too fast.

references.title: NHS: Type 2 diabetes – symptoms and diagnosis
NICE NG28: Type 2 diabetes in adults: management

hba1c.specimen: Venous blood in an EDTA tube; fingerprick point-of-care devices in some clinics
hba1c.resultType: Numeric, read against diagnostic and target thresholds

quick.sample: Blood from a vein, no fasting
quick.usedFor: Diagnosing type 2 diabetes, monitoring diabetes control
quick.measures: Glycated haemoglobin, the average blood glucose of the previous two to three months

components.name: HbA1c
components.measures: Percentage of haemoglobin with glucose attached, reported in mmol/mol
components.high: Diabetes, prediabetes; falsely high with iron deficiency and slow red-cell turnover
components.low: Improving control; falsely low with haemolysis, blood loss, transfusion, pregnancy

hba1c.rangeNote: HbA1c is not read against a laboratory reference interval but against internationally agreed diagnostic thresholds and individualised treatment targets. Conditions that change red-cell lifespan make the value unreliable whatever the threshold.

thresholds.name: Diabetes
thresholds.context: Diagnosis of type 2 diabetes; repeated to confirm unless symptoms are present. Not valid in conditions that affect red cells

source.title: NHS: Type 2 diabetes – symptoms and diagnosis

thresholds.name: Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (prediabetes)
thresholds.context: High risk of type 2 diabetes; lifestyle intervention offered

source.title: NICE PH38: Type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk

thresholds.name: Treatment target (diet or a single drug not causing hypoglycaemia)
thresholds.context: Adults with type 2 diabetes managed by lifestyle or one agent; individualised

source.title: NICE NG28: Type 2 diabetes in adults: management

thresholds.name: Treatment target (a drug that can cause hypoglycaemia)
thresholds.context: Adults with type 2 diabetes on treatment associated with hypoglycaemia; relaxed for older or frail people

source.title: NICE NG28: Type 2 diabetes in adults: management

factors: Anything that shortens or lengthens red-cell life: haemolysis, blood loss, transfusion, iron deficiency, kidney failure, pregnancy
Haemoglobin variants, which interfere with some assay methods
Very recent changes in glucose control, which the value has not yet caught up with
Erythropoietin and iron treatment
cannotTell: Day-to-day swings in glucose or episodes of hypoglycaemia
Type 1 diabetes at presentation, where glucose rises too fast for HbA1c to reflect it
Whether control is good in someone whose red cells turn over abnormally
hba1c.medicinesNote: Glucose-lowering medicines lower it; corticosteroids and some antipsychotics raise it by raising glucose; iron and erythropoietin treatment can shift it independently of glucose.

liver-function-tests.name: Liver function tests
liver-function-tests.what: A panel of enzymes and proteins that together show whether liver cells are injured, whether bile is flowing, and whether the liver is still doing its manufacturing job.

measures.meaning: Enzymes that leak from damaged liver cells (hepatitis, fatty liver, drugs, alcohol).
Rise when bile ducts are blocked or irritated; ALP also comes from bone.
The pigment from broken-down red cells; high levels cause jaundice.
The main blood protein the liver makes; falls in chronic liver disease and malnutrition.
Clotting factors are made in the liver, so slow clotting means poor synthetic function.

whyOrdered: Jaundice, dark urine, pale stools
Abdominal pain, nausea, itching
Heavy alcohol use or viral hepatitis risk
Monitoring statins, methotrexate, antiepileptics and many other drugs
Fatty liver in obesity and diabetes
liver-function-tests.preparation: None, though fasting improves consistency for some labs.

interpretation.finding: ALT and AST much higher than ALP
interpretation.meaning: Hepatocellular injury: viral hepatitis, drugs, fatty liver, alcohol

interpretation.finding: ALP and GGT high with raised bilirubin
interpretation.meaning: Cholestasis: gallstone in the bile duct, pancreatic tumour, some drugs
Loss of synthetic function: cirrhosis or acute liver failure
Often Gilbert syndrome, a harmless inherited variation

liver-function-tests.limitations: Despite the name, they mostly detect damage rather than measure function; a normal panel does not exclude cirrhosis. Muscle injury raises AST, bone growth raises ALP.
liver-function-tests.resultType: A panel of numeric values, each with a laboratory reference interval; the pattern across the panel matters more than any single value

quick.usedFor: Jaundice, abdominal symptoms, alcohol, fatty liver, drug monitoring
quick.measures: Liver enzymes, bilirubin and albumin: injury, bile flow and synthesis

components.name: ALT
components.measures: Enzyme released from injured liver cells
components.high: Hepatitis, fatty liver, alcohol, drugs, congestion

components.name: AST
components.measures: Enzyme from liver, muscle, heart and red cells
components.high: Liver injury (alcohol-related if AST exceeds ALT), muscle injury, haemolysis

components.name: Alkaline phosphatase
components.measures: Enzyme from bile ducts and bone
components.high: Cholestasis, bone disease, growth, pregnancy

components.name: GGT
components.measures: Enzyme induced by cholestasis, alcohol and drugs
components.high: Bile-duct obstruction, alcohol, fatty liver, enzyme-inducing drugs

components.name: Bilirubin
components.measures: Breakdown product of haemoglobin processed by the liver
components.high: Haemolysis, Gilbert syndrome, hepatitis, bile-duct obstruction

components.name: Albumin
components.measures: Main protein made by the liver
components.high: Dehydration
components.low: Cirrhosis, inflammation, malnutrition, kidney or gut protein loss

components.name: Prothrombin time / INR (often added)
components.measures: Clotting factor production by the liver
components.high: Severe liver injury, cirrhosis, vitamin K deficiency, warfarin

liver-function-tests.rangeNote: Each enzyme has its own laboratory reference interval that varies by method, sex and age (alkaline phosphatase is naturally high in growing children). A mild elevation of one enzyme is common and often needs only a repeat; the pattern (hepatocellular versus cholestatic), the size of the rise and the trend guide what happens next.
factors: Alcohol in the preceding days and weeks
Obesity and fatty liver, which cause the commonest mild abnormalities
Strenuous exercise and muscle injury (AST, and to a lesser extent ALT)
Pregnancy (ALP), growth in childhood, fasting (bilirubin in Gilbert syndrome)
Many medicines and herbal supplements
cannotTell: How much scarring (fibrosis) the liver has: a normal panel does not exclude cirrhosis, and fibrosis is assessed with scores such as FIB-4, elastography or biopsy
The cause of liver injury without further tests (viral serology, autoimmune antibodies, iron studies, ultrasound)
True 'function' in most cases: the enzymes show injury, and only albumin and clotting reflect synthesis
liver-function-tests.medicinesNote: Statins, paracetamol in overdose, antibiotics such as flucloxacillin and co-amoxiclav, antiepileptics, methotrexate, antifungals, antituberculous drugs and some herbal products can raise liver enzymes; oral contraceptives and anabolic steroids can cause cholestasis.

kidney-function-tests.name: Kidney function tests
kidney-function-tests.what: Creatinine and urea are waste products the kidneys should clear; how much builds up in blood shows how well they are filtering. Creatinine is converted into an estimated filtration rate (eGFR), the standard measure of kidney function.

measures.meaning: Muscle waste cleared by filtration; rises as kidney function falls. Depends on muscle mass.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate in mL/min/1.73 m²; over 90 normal, under 60 for three months defines chronic kidney disease, under 15 is kidney failure.
Protein waste; rises with poor kidney function but also dehydration, bleeding into the gut and high protein intake.
Usually reported together; potassium climbs dangerously when kidneys fail.

whyOrdered: Screening people with diabetes or high blood pressure
Before contrast scans and many drugs
Swelling, reduced urine, tiredness, nausea
Dehydration, vomiting, diarrhoea
Monitoring ACE inhibitors, diuretics, lithium and NSAIDs
kidney-function-tests.how: Venous blood; usually paired with a urine protein test.
kidney-function-tests.preparation: None; avoid heavy exercise or a large meat meal the day before if possible.

interpretation.finding: Rising creatinine over hours to days
interpretation.meaning: Acute kidney injury: dehydration, sepsis, obstruction, drugs; usually reversible if caught
Chronic kidney disease, staged 3-5 by the value
Dehydration or gut bleeding rather than kidney damage

kidney-function-tests.limitations: eGFR is an estimate; it is inaccurate at extremes of muscle mass, in pregnancy and in rapidly changing illness. Half of kidney function can be lost before creatinine leaves the normal range.

references.title: NICE NG203: Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management

kidney-function-tests.specimen: Venous blood (serum); usually paired with a urine sample
kidney-function-tests.resultType: A panel of numeric values with laboratory reference intervals, plus an eGFR read against staging thresholds

quick.usedFor: Kidney function, dehydration, electrolyte balance, drug monitoring
quick.measures: Urea, creatinine, eGFR, sodium and potassium

components.name: Creatinine
components.measures: Muscle waste product cleared by the kidney
components.high: Reduced filtration, dehydration, high muscle mass

components.name: eGFR
components.measures: Estimated filtration rate
components.high: Normal in the young
components.low: Chronic kidney disease, acute kidney injury

components.name: Urea
components.measures: Protein waste made by the liver, cleared by the kidney
components.high: Kidney impairment, dehydration, gut bleeding, high-protein diet, steroids

components.name: Sodium
components.measures: Main extracellular ion; reflects water balance
components.high: Water loss without replacement
components.low: Excess water, SIADH, thiazides, heart or liver failure

components.name: Potassium
components.measures: Main intracellular ion; sets cardiac excitability
components.high: Kidney impairment, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, haemolysed sample

kidney-function-tests.rangeNote: Urea, creatinine and the electrolytes each have a laboratory reference interval; the eGFR is read against chronic kidney disease staging thresholds (see the creatinine and eGFR page) and requires two results at least three months apart before a diagnosis is made.
factors: Hydration, recent vomiting or diarrhoea and intravenous fluids
Muscle mass, diet (meat), creatine supplements and exercise
Sample handling: a squeezed, delayed or haemolysed sample raises potassium
Medicines: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, lithium
cannotTell: The cause of kidney impairment or whether it is reversible
Protein or blood in the urine, which need urine tests
Total body potassium or sodium, only their blood concentration
kidney-function-tests.medicinesNote: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium-sparing diuretics raise potassium and creatinine; loop and thiazide diuretics lower potassium and sodium; NSAIDs, lithium and contrast can reduce filtration; trimethoprim raises creatinine without harming the kidney.

lipid-profile.name: Lipid profile
lipid-profile.what: Measures the fats carried in blood: total cholesterol, LDL ('bad', deposited in artery walls), HDL ('good', carried away for disposal) and triglycerides. Used mainly to estimate and manage the risk of heart attack and stroke.

measures.meaning: Ideally below 5 mmol/L for the general population.
The particle that builds atherosclerotic plaque; the main treatment target.
Higher is protective; above 1.0 in men and 1.2 in women.
Fat from food and the liver; very high levels can cause pancreatitis.
Total minus HDL: all the harmful particles together.

whyOrdered: Cardiovascular risk assessment from age 40, earlier with family history
Known heart disease, stroke or peripheral artery disease
Diabetes, kidney disease, high blood pressure
Monitoring statin treatment
Xanthomas or very early heart disease in a family (familial hypercholesterolaemia)
lipid-profile.how: Venous blood, fasting no longer required for most purposes.
lipid-profile.preparation: Usually none; a fasting sample if triglycerides are very high.

interpretation.meaning: Raised risk; combined with age, blood pressure and smoking into a 10-year risk score to decide on statins

interpretation.finding: Total cholesterol above 7.5 with family history
interpretation.meaning: Possible familial hypercholesterolaemia; genetic testing and family screening
Risk of pancreatitis; look for alcohol, diabetes, drugs

lipid-profile.limitations: Cholesterol is one risk factor among several; the numbers matter less than the overall risk. Acute illness lowers cholesterol for weeks.

references.title: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification
NICE CG71: Familial hypercholesterolaemia: identification and management

lipid-profile.resultType: A panel of numeric values used in risk calculators and against treatment targets

quick.sample: Blood from a vein, fasting usually not needed
quick.usedFor: Cardiovascular risk assessment, familial hypercholesterolaemia, statin monitoring
quick.measures: Total, LDL, HDL and non-HDL cholesterol and triglycerides

components.name: Total cholesterol
components.measures: All cholesterol carried in blood
components.high: Diet, inherited disorders, hypothyroidism, kidney and liver disease

components.name: LDL cholesterol
components.measures: Cholesterol in low-density lipoprotein (usually calculated)
components.high: Familial hypercholesterolaemia, diet, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome

components.name: HDL cholesterol
components.measures: Cholesterol in high-density lipoprotein
components.high: Exercise, moderate alcohol, oestrogen
components.low: Obesity, inactivity, smoking, diabetes, high triglycerides

components.name: Non-HDL cholesterol
components.measures: Total minus HDL: all the atherogenic particles
components.high: As for LDL; the value UK guidance uses for targets

components.name: Triglycerides
components.measures: Blood fat carried in chylomicrons and VLDL
components.high: Recent meal, alcohol, obesity, diabetes, some medicines, inherited disorders

lipid-profile.rangeNote: Cholesterol values are not judged against a laboratory reference interval, because the 'average' value in the population is already associated with cardiovascular disease. Instead they feed a risk calculator (QRISK in the UK) and are compared with guideline targets once treatment starts.

thresholds.name: Statin treatment goal (secondary prevention)
thresholds.value: LDL cholesterol 2.0 or below, or non-HDL cholesterol 2.6 or below
thresholds.context: People with established cardiovascular disease on statin treatment; escalate treatment if not achieved

source.title: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification

thresholds.name: Statin treatment goal (primary prevention)
thresholds.value: more than 40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol
thresholds.context: People started on a statin for primary prevention, measured at 3 months

source.title: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification

thresholds.name: Consider familial hypercholesterolaemia
thresholds.value: total cholesterol above 7.5 (adults) with a family history of premature heart disease
thresholds.context: Adults; prompts formal assessment with Simon Broome or Dutch Lipid Clinic criteria and possible genetic testing

source.title: NICE CG71: Familial hypercholesterolaemia: identification and management

thresholds.name: Pancreatitis risk
thresholds.context: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia; urgent specialist referral in UK guidance

source.title: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification

factors: A recent meal and alcohol raise triglycerides; fasting is only needed when triglycerides are very high
Acute illness, surgery and heart attack lower cholesterol for weeks
Weight change, pregnancy and the menstrual cycle
Untreated hypothyroidism raises LDL; check thyroid function before treating an unexpectedly high result
cannotTell: A person's overall cardiovascular risk on its own (age, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes and family history are combined with it)
Whether arteries already contain plaque (that needs imaging)
Which lipid-lowering treatment is appropriate
lipid-profile.medicinesNote: Statins, ezetimibe, fibrates and PCSK9 inhibitors lower values; corticosteroids, some antiretrovirals, isotretinoin, thiazides and beta blockers can raise cholesterol or triglycerides.

electrolytes.name: Electrolytes
electrolytes.what: The dissolved salts that set the water content of the body and the electrical behaviour of nerves, muscle and the heart: sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, calcium, magnesium and phosphate.

measures.meaning: Governs water balance; 135-145 mmol/L. Low sodium is the commonest electrolyte disorder in hospital.
3.5-5.0 mmol/L. High or low levels cause dangerous heart rhythms.
The blood's main buffer; low in acidosis, high in alkalosis.
Corrected for albumin; high in parathyroid overactivity and cancer, low after thyroid surgery and in vitamin D deficiency.
Fall with malnutrition, alcohol and refeeding; matter for heart rhythm and muscle.

whyOrdered: Confusion, weakness, seizures, palpitations
Vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration
Kidney disease and diuretic treatment
Before and after surgery
Endocrine disease (adrenal, parathyroid)
electrolytes.how: Venous blood; potassium is falsely high if the sample is squeezed or delayed.

interpretation.meaning: Often too much water relative to salt: diuretics, heart or liver failure, SIADH, excess drinking
Kidney failure, ACE inhibitors and spironolactone, tissue breakdown; needs an ECG
Vomiting, diarrhoea, loop diuretics, steroid excess
Primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy in most adults

electrolytes.limitations: Blood levels do not always reflect total body stores (potassium is mostly inside cells). Haemolysed samples give spurious potassium.

thyroid-function-tests.name: Thyroid function tests
thyroid-function-tests.what: TSH from the pituitary and the thyroid hormones T4 and T3 measured together. Because the pituitary reacts to tiny changes in hormone level, TSH is the most sensitive single indicator of thyroid status.

measures.meaning: Thyroid-stimulating hormone; high when the thyroid is underactive, suppressed when it is overactive.
The main hormone the thyroid releases; low in hypothyroidism, high in hyperthyroidism.
The active hormone; added when TSH is low to detect T3 toxicosis.
TPO antibodies mark autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis; TSH-receptor antibodies mark Graves disease.

whyOrdered: Tiredness, weight change, feeling cold or hot, palpitations, anxiety
A goitre or neck lump
Atrial fibrillation, high cholesterol, depression
Monitoring levothyroxine or antithyroid drugs
Amiodarone or lithium treatment, pregnancy planning
thyroid-function-tests.how: Venous blood, any time of day (take levothyroxine after the sample).
thyroid-function-tests.preparation: None; biotin supplements can interfere and should be paused for two days.

interpretation.meaning: Primary hypothyroidism
Subclinical hypothyroidism; treat if symptomatic, pregnant or TSH very high

interpretation.finding: Low TSH, high T4 or T3
interpretation.meaning: Hyperthyroidism: Graves disease, toxic nodules, thyroiditis
Pituitary (secondary) failure, or recent overtreatment

thyroid-function-tests.limitations: Acute illness and some drugs disturb results ('sick euthyroid'); repeat once recovered. TSH lags six weeks behind a dose change.

references.title: NICE NG145: Thyroid disease: assessment and management

thyroid-function-tests.resultType: Numeric values with laboratory reference intervals, read as a pattern

quick.usedFor: Suspected thyroid disease, monitoring treatment, pituitary disease
quick.measures: TSH with free T4 and sometimes free T3 and thyroid antibodies

components.name: TSH
components.measures: Pituitary drive to the thyroid
components.high: Hypothyroidism

components.name: Free T4
components.measures: Unbound thyroxine
components.high: Hyperthyroidism, excess levothyroxine

components.name: Free T3
components.measures: Unbound triiodothyronine, the active hormone
components.high: Hyperthyroidism (T3 toxicosis)

components.name: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies (when requested)
components.measures: Autoimmune thyroid disease
components.high: Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease; predicts progression of subclinical hypothyroidism

thyroid-function-tests.rangeNote: Each hormone has a laboratory reference interval that depends on the assay and, for TSH, on age and pregnancy. The combination of values is what matters: a single hormone outside its interval is interpreted with the others.
factors: Acute and severe illness (sick euthyroid pattern)
Biotin supplements interfering with the assay
Pregnancy and the first trimester rise in hCG
Amiodarone, lithium, glucocorticoids, dopamine, some antiepileptics
Levothyroxine timing and absorption
cannotTell: The cause of thyroid dysfunction without antibodies, ultrasound or uptake scans
Whether a nodule is present or cancerous
Thyroid status reliably during severe non-thyroidal illness
thyroid-function-tests.medicinesNote: Levothyroxine and antithyroid drugs are the intended influences; amiodarone, lithium, interferons and immune checkpoint inhibitors can cause thyroid dysfunction; iron, calcium and proton pump inhibitors reduce levothyroxine absorption.

hormone-tests.name: Hormone tests
hormone-tests.what: Blood levels of hormones and related chemicals, interpreted against the time of day, the cycle and the level of the controlling hormone from the pituitary. Includes cortisol, sex hormones, prolactin, growth hormone, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and, by convention on this site, uric acid.

measures.meaning: The stress hormone from the adrenal cortex; highest at 9 am. Low in Addison disease, high in Cushing syndrome.
Sex hormones; measured with LH and FSH from the pituitary to tell gland failure from pituitary failure.
Raised by pituitary tumours, stress, many drugs and pregnancy; causes milk production and lost periods.
Control calcium and bone; a high PTH with high calcium is primary hyperparathyroidism.
The waste product that crystallises in gout; above 360 micromol/L raises risk, targets in gout are below 300-360.

whyOrdered: Suspected adrenal, pituitary or gonadal disease
Osteoporosis and calcium problems
Gout diagnosis and treatment targets
Infertility, missed periods, erectile dysfunction, hair changes
Assessing pituitary function after tumours or surgery
hormone-tests.how: Venous blood, often at a set time (9 am cortisol, early morning testosterone) or after a stimulation or suppression drug.
hormone-tests.preparation: Depends on the test; some need fasting, timing to the menstrual cycle, or stopping biotin and steroids.

interpretation.meaning: Adrenal insufficiency; confirmed with a synacthen stimulation test
Primary hyperparathyroidism, usually a single adenoma
Testicular failure; low LH points to the pituitary instead
Supports gout, but can be normal during an attack

hormone-tests.limitations: Hormones pulse and cycle; a single random level is often uninterpretable. Dynamic tests (stimulate or suppress the gland, then measure) are needed to prove most diagnoses.

urinalysis.name: Urinalysis
urinalysis.what: A plastic strip with chemical pads dipped into a fresh urine sample. In sixty seconds it screens for infection, blood, protein, glucose, ketones and how concentrated the urine is, with microscopy for cells and crystals when needed.

measures.meaning: White cells and bacterial nitrite together point to a urinary infection.
Infection, stones, tumours or kidney inflammation; persistent invisible blood needs investigation.
A sign of kidney damage, especially in diabetes and high blood pressure; confirmed with a lab ratio.
Glucose spills over when blood sugar is high; ketones mean fat is being burned (starvation, diabetic ketoacidosis).
How concentrated the urine is and its acidity, useful in dehydration and stone disease.

whyOrdered: Burning, frequency or urgency (suspected infection)
Abdominal or loin pain
Screening in diabetes, high blood pressure and pregnancy
Unexplained fever in children and older adults
Kidney disease monitoring
urinalysis.how: Midstream urine into a clean pot; dipped immediately or sent for microscopy and culture.
urinalysis.preparation: Clean the area and catch the middle of the stream; first-morning samples are most concentrated.

interpretation.meaning: Likely urinary tract infection; a culture confirms the organism
Glomerular disease: needs kidney function tests and specialist review
Check blood glucose for diabetes (or SGLT2 inhibitor treatment)
Possible diabetic ketoacidosis, an emergency

urinalysis.limitations: Dipsticks in older adults often show bacteria without infection (asymptomatic bacteriuria) and should not drive antibiotics on their own. Menstrual blood and vigorous exercise cause false positives for blood.

references.title: NICE NG203: Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management

urinalysis.specimen: Midstream urine in a clean container, tested fresh
urinalysis.resultType: Semi-quantitative dipstick pads (negative to 3+), specific gravity and pH, plus microscopy when requested

quick.usedFor: Urinary infection, kidney disease, diabetes screening, pregnancy checks
quick.measures: Chemical pads for leucocytes, nitrite, blood, protein, glucose, ketones, concentration and acidity; cells and crystals on microscopy

components.name: Leucocyte esterase
components.measures: White cells in the urine
components.high: Urinary infection, inflammation of the urinary tract, contamination

components.name: Nitrite
components.measures: Bacteria that convert nitrate to nitrite
components.high: Infection with common gut bacteria (E. coli); a negative result does not exclude infection

components.name: Blood
components.measures: Red cells or free haemoglobin/myoglobin
components.high: Infection, stones, glomerular disease, tumours, menstruation, exercise, muscle breakdown

components.name: Protein
components.measures: Mainly albumin leaking from the kidney
components.high: Kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, pre-eclampsia, fever, exercise; confirmed with an albumin-to-creatinine ratio

components.name: Glucose
components.measures: Glucose spilling over from blood
components.high: Diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitor treatment, pregnancy, rare kidney tubular disorders

components.name: Ketones
components.measures: Fat-breakdown products
components.high: Fasting, diabetic ketoacidosis, low-carbohydrate diets, vomiting

components.name: Specific gravity and pH
components.measures: Concentration and acidity of the urine
components.high: Dehydration (high specific gravity); alkaline urine with some infections and diets
components.low: Dilute urine: high fluid intake, diabetes insipidus, kidney concentrating defects

urinalysis.rangeNote: Dipstick results are graded rather than measured, and a positive pad is a screening finding: infection is confirmed by symptoms and culture, protein by a laboratory albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and blood by microscopy and, where persistent, further investigation.
factors: Contamination from the genital area or menstrual blood
Delay before testing (bacteria multiply, cells break down) and exposure of the strip to air
Very dilute or very concentrated urine
Vitamin C can cause false negatives for blood and glucose; some antibiotics and dyes discolour the sample
Vigorous exercise, fever and dehydration cause transient protein or blood
cannotTell: Whether bacteria in the urine are causing illness: older adults often carry bacteria without infection and should not be treated on the dipstick alone
How much protein is leaking (quantified by an albumin-to-creatinine ratio)
The cause of blood in the urine, which needs microscopy, imaging and sometimes cystoscopy
urinalysis.medicinesNote: SGLT2 inhibitors put glucose in the urine by design; nitrofurantoin and some other drugs discolour it; vitamin C causes false negatives; NSAIDs and lithium can cause protein or blood.

urine-culture.name: Urine culture
urine-culture.what: A urine sample is spread on culture plates and incubated for 24-48 hours to grow any bacteria, identify them and test which antibiotics kill them. It turns a dipstick suspicion into a proven infection with a targeted treatment.

measures.meaning: 100,000 or more colony-forming units per mL of a single organism is significant; lower counts count in symptomatic patients and catheter samples.
E. coli causes most infections; Proteus suggests stones; Staphylococcus saprophyticus in young women; mixed growth usually means contamination.
Which antibiotics the organism is sensitive or resistant to.

whyOrdered: Infection in men, children, pregnancy and anyone with a catheter or kidney disease
Infections that keep coming back or fail treatment
Suspected kidney infection or sepsis from a urinary source
Before urological surgery
urine-culture.how: Midstream sample in a sterile pot (or from a fresh catheter); refrigerate if it cannot reach the lab within hours.
urine-culture.preparation: Collect before starting antibiotics whenever possible.

interpretation.finding: Pure growth of E. coli, sensitive to nitrofurantoin
interpretation.meaning: Confirmed infection; treat with the narrowest effective antibiotic
Probably contaminated; repeat with careful collection
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: treat only in pregnancy or before urological procedures

urine-culture.limitations: Results take two days, so treatment often starts empirically. Antibiotics taken beforehand can sterilise the sample.

urine-protein.name: Urine protein
urine-protein.what: Healthy kidney filters hold back almost all protein. Measuring albumin leaking into urine, corrected for how dilute the sample is, detects kidney damage years before blood tests change, particularly in diabetes and high blood pressure.

measures.meaning: Below 3 mg/mmol normal; 3-30 moderately raised (formerly microalbuminuria); above 30 severe. Combined with eGFR to stage kidney disease.
All proteins, used when large amounts leak (nephrotic range above 300 mg/mmol).
The old gold standard, now rarely needed.

whyOrdered: Yearly in diabetes
High blood pressure, kidney disease, lupus
Frothy urine or unexplained swelling
Pregnancy with high blood pressure (pre-eclampsia)
Staging chronic kidney disease and deciding on ACE inhibitors and SGLT2 inhibitors
urine-protein.preparation: Avoid hard exercise the day before; repeat if there is infection or fever.

interpretation.meaning: Kidney damage: start or intensify an ACE inhibitor/ARB, control blood pressure and glucose

interpretation.finding: Nephrotic-range protein with low albumin and swelling
interpretation.meaning: Nephrotic syndrome, needs a kidney biopsy in adults
Glomerulonephritis; urgent specialist referral

urine-protein.limitations: Exercise, fever, infection and standing for long periods raise protein transiently; two out of three samples must be positive to confirm.

pregnancy-test.name: Pregnancy test
pregnancy-test.what: Detects human chorionic gonadotropin, a hormone made by the placenta from about a week after implantation. Urine tests give a yes/no answer; a blood test gives a number that should double every two days in a healthy early pregnancy.

measures.meaning: Positive from around the first missed period; modern tests detect 20-25 IU/L.
Quantitative; used to track ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage and molar pregnancy, and some tumours.

whyOrdered: A missed period, nausea, breast tenderness
Abdominal pain or bleeding in any woman of reproductive age (to exclude ectopic pregnancy)
Before X-rays, CT, surgery and many drugs
Monitoring after ectopic pregnancy or molar pregnancy treatment
pregnancy-test.how: A drop of urine on a test strip, ideally first-morning; or a venous blood sample.
pregnancy-test.preparation: None; testing before the missed period risks a false negative.

interpretation.meaning: Pregnant, almost always; an ultrasound from 6 weeks locates the pregnancy

interpretation.finding: Positive test with pain or bleeding
interpretation.meaning: Ectopic pregnancy must be excluded urgently
Failing or ectopic pregnancy

pregnancy-test.limitations: False negatives when tested too early or with very dilute urine; rare false positives from fertility drugs, some tumours and recent pregnancy loss.

ecg.name: Electrocardiogram
ecg.what: Ten sticky electrodes on the chest and limbs record the heart's electrical activity from twelve angles over ten seconds. The tracing shows rhythm, rate, the direction of electrical spread and signs of muscle strain, damage or blocked blood supply.

measures.meaning: Normal sinus rhythm 60-100 per minute; irregular with no P waves in atrial fibrillation.
Atrial activation and the delay at the AV node; a long PR is heart block.
Ventricular activation; wide when conduction is blocked in a bundle branch.
Repolarisation; ST elevation is the signature of an acute heart attack, ST depression of ischaemia or strain.
Total activation time; prolonged by drugs and electrolyte problems, risking dangerous rhythms.

whyOrdered: Chest pain (within 10 minutes of arrival)
Palpitations, blackouts, breathlessness
Screening before surgery or in athletes
Electrolyte problems and drug monitoring
Suspected pulmonary embolism, pericarditis, heart failure
ecg.how: Lie still for a minute while the machine prints; painless, no electricity goes into the body.
ecg.preparation: None; chest hair may be shaved for contact.

interpretation.finding: ST elevation in two adjacent leads
interpretation.meaning: STEMI: an artery is blocked, needs emergency angioplasty

interpretation.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves
interpretation.meaning: Atrial fibrillation
High potassium, needs immediate treatment
Reassuring but does not exclude a heart attack or intermittent rhythm problems

ecg.limitations: A ten-second snapshot: intermittent arrhythmias need longer monitoring, and a third of heart attacks have a normal first ECG.
ecg.specimen: None: a recording of the heart's electrical activity from skin electrodes
ecg.resultType: A tracing read for rate, rhythm, intervals and waveform changes, with an automated interpretation checked by a clinician

quick.sample: No sample; ten electrodes on the chest and limbs
quick.usedFor: Chest pain, palpitations, blackouts, rhythm problems, screening
quick.measures: The heart's electrical rhythm and conduction from twelve angles over ten seconds

components.name: Rate and rhythm
components.measures: How fast and how regularly the heart beats
components.high: Sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or flutter, supraventricular and ventricular tachycardias
components.low: Sinus bradycardia, heart block, sick sinus syndrome

components.name: P wave and PR interval
components.measures: Atrial activation and conduction through the AV node
components.high: Long PR: first-degree heart block

components.name: QRS complex
components.measures: Ventricular activation
components.high: Wide QRS: bundle branch block, ventricular rhythms, high potassium; tall complexes: hypertrophy; Q waves: old infarction
components.low: Small complexes: obesity, pericardial fluid, lung disease

components.name: ST segment and T wave
components.measures: Ventricular recovery; the part most changed by ischaemia
components.high: ST elevation: acute infarction (STEMI) or pericarditis; tall T waves: high potassium
components.low: ST depression and T inversion: ischaemia, strain, digoxin, low potassium

components.name: QT interval
components.measures: Total time for ventricular activation and recovery, corrected for heart rate
components.high: Long QT: inherited syndromes, many medicines, low potassium, magnesium or calcium; risk of dangerous rhythms
components.low: Short QT: rare inherited syndromes, high calcium

ecg.rangeNote: An ECG is interpreted against standard interval limits and waveform criteria rather than a laboratory range; the automated report on the machine is a starting point that a clinician confirms or overrules, ideally by comparison with a previous tracing.
factors: Electrode placement, movement, shivering and electrical interference
Body shape, lung disease and pericardial fluid change voltages
Electrolyte levels (potassium, calcium, magnesium) and many medicines
Heart rate, which changes the corrected QT
Timing: a tracing between episodes of an intermittent arrhythmia is often normal
cannotTell: Whether a heart attack has occurred when the first tracing is normal (a third of infarctions are); serial ECGs and troponin are needed
How well the heart pumps or whether the valves work (echocardiography)
Whether the coronary arteries are narrowed when the person is at rest (stress testing or angiography)
Intermittent rhythm problems that were not happening during the ten seconds recorded
ecg.medicinesNote: Many medicines prolong the QT interval (some antibiotics including macrolides, antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiemetics); digoxin, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers slow conduction; sodium channel blockers widen the QRS.

echocardiogram.name: Echocardiogram
echocardiogram.what: An ultrasound of the beating heart. It shows the size and thickness of the chambers, how strongly the ventricles pump, whether the valves open and close properly, and the pressures inside, all in real time and without radiation.

measures.meaning: The fraction of blood the left ventricle ejects each beat; 55% or more is normal, below 40% is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
Narrowing (stenosis) or leaking (regurgitation), graded by Doppler flow.
A segment that does not move marks scar from a previous heart attack.
Dilated in heart failure, thickened in high blood pressure and cardiomyopathy.
Fluid around the heart (effusion) and whether it compresses the chambers.

whyOrdered: Breathlessness or raised BNP (heart failure)
A murmur or suspected valve disease
After a heart attack
Atrial fibrillation, stroke (looking for a source of clots)
Suspected endocarditis, pericardial fluid, congenital heart disease
echocardiogram.how: Lying on the left side, a probe with gel is moved over the chest for 20-40 minutes. A transoesophageal echo passes a probe down the gullet for clearer views, with sedation.
echocardiogram.preparation: None for the standard test; fasting for the transoesophageal version.

interpretation.meaning: Significantly reduced pumping; start heart-failure treatment
Valve replacement when symptoms appear
Coronary disease with previous infarction
Heart failure and valve disease effectively excluded

echocardiogram.limitations: Image quality falls with obesity and lung disease. Coronary arteries themselves are not seen; a stress echo or angiogram is needed for that.

references.title: NICE NG106: Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management

echocardiogram.specimen: None: ultrasound images of the beating heart
echocardiogram.resultType: Measurements (ejection fraction, chamber sizes, wall thickness, valve gradients) with a structured report

quick.sample: No sample; a probe with gel on the chest, 20-40 minutes
quick.usedFor: Heart failure, murmurs and valve disease, after a heart attack, stroke work-up
quick.measures: Heart structure, pumping function, valve function and pressures in real time

components.name: Left ventricular ejection fraction
components.measures: Percentage of blood the left ventricle ejects each beat
components.high: Hyperdynamic states (sepsis, anaemia, thyrotoxicosis)
components.low: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, previous infarction, cardiomyopathy

components.name: Wall motion
components.measures: Whether each segment of muscle contracts normally
components.high: Not applicable
components.low: Regional abnormality: infarction or ischaemia in a coronary territory

components.name: Chamber size and wall thickness
components.measures: Dilatation or hypertrophy of the atria and ventricles
components.high: Dilated: heart failure, valve leaks, atrial fibrillation; thick walls: hypertension, aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

components.name: Valve function
components.measures: Narrowing (stenosis) or leaking (regurgitation) of each valve, graded by Doppler
components.high: Severe stenosis or regurgitation may need repair or replacement

components.name: Diastolic function and filling pressures
components.measures: How the ventricle relaxes and fills
components.high: Raised filling pressures: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension, older age

components.name: Pericardium and estimated pulmonary pressure
components.measures: Fluid around the heart; right-heart pressures
components.high: Pericardial effusion; pulmonary hypertension from lung disease, clots or left-heart disease

echocardiogram.rangeNote: Measurements are compared with published reference values adjusted for body size, age and sex, and graded (mild, moderate, severe) using society criteria; the report is a clinical interpretation, not a laboratory range.
factors: Image quality: obesity, lung disease and chest-wall shape limit the acoustic window (a transoesophageal echo or contrast may be needed)
Heart rate and rhythm at the time (atrial fibrillation makes measurements variable)
Blood pressure and fluid status on the day
Operator experience and machine settings
cannotTell: Whether the coronary arteries are narrowed (stress echo, CT or angiography)
The heart's electrical rhythm over time (ECG and monitoring)
The cause of breathlessness when the heart is normal
echocardiogram.medicinesNote: Heart-failure medicines can improve ejection fraction over months; beta blockers and rate control change measurements in atrial fibrillation; some chemotherapy (anthracyclines, trastuzumab) is monitored with serial echocardiograms.

stress-test.name: Cardiac stress test
stress-test.what: The heart is made to work hard, by treadmill or bicycle exercise or by a drug that mimics exercise, while its electrical activity, images or blood flow are recorded. A narrowed coronary artery that copes at rest fails under load, revealing itself as ECG change, a segment of muscle that stops moving, or a patch that does not take up tracer.

measures.meaning: ST depression, arrhythmia or a fall in blood pressure signal ischaemia.
Minutes achieved and heart rate reached; a strong predictor of prognosis in itself.
A segment that moves at rest but not under stress marks a significant narrowing.
Reduced tracer uptake under stress that recovers at rest = reversible ischaemia; fixed defect = scar.

whyOrdered: Chest pain on exertion with an intermediate probability of coronary disease
Assessing how much a known narrowing matters
After a heart attack or angioplasty, before cardiac rehabilitation
Exercise-induced palpitations or blackouts
stress-test.how: Electrodes and blood pressure cuff on; the treadmill speeds up every three minutes until target heart rate, symptoms or ECG change. Imaging versions add ultrasound or a radioactive tracer.
stress-test.preparation: Light meal only; comfortable shoes; some heart drugs (beta blockers) are paused on instruction.

interpretation.finding: Marked ST depression early in exercise
interpretation.meaning: High-risk coronary disease; proceed to angiography

interpretation.finding: Good exercise capacity with no changes
interpretation.meaning: Low risk; significant disease unlikely
Viable muscle with restricted supply, likely to benefit from revascularisation

stress-test.limitations: Exercise ECG alone misses a fifth of disease and gives false positives, especially in women and with abnormal resting ECGs; CT coronary angiography is now the first test in many guidelines.

holter-monitor.name: Ambulatory ECG monitoring
holter-monitor.what: A portable recorder worn for 24 hours to two weeks (or an implanted loop recorder for up to three years) that captures the heart's rhythm during normal life, catching the intermittent arrhythmias a ten-second ECG misses.

measures.meaning: Every beat is recorded and analysed; runs of atrial fibrillation, pauses and extra beats are counted.
The wearer presses a button or keeps a diary so symptoms can be matched to the tracing at that moment.
Slowest and fastest rates, including during sleep.

whyOrdered: Palpitations that come and go
Unexplained blackouts or falls
Looking for atrial fibrillation after a stroke
Checking a pacemaker or drug treatment is controlling a rhythm
Suspected heart block
holter-monitor.how: Three to five chest electrodes lead to a small recorder on a belt, or a single adhesive patch; normal activities continue except bathing. Implantable recorders are injected under the skin of the chest.

interpretation.meaning: Diagnosis made; consider anticoagulation and rate or rhythm control

interpretation.finding: Pause of more than 3 seconds with dizziness
interpretation.meaning: Symptomatic bradycardia; likely pacemaker
Palpitations are not due to an arrhythmia; reassuring

holter-monitor.limitations: Only useful if symptoms occur during the recording; rare events need longer monitoring or an implanted device.

spirometry.name: Spirometry
spirometry.what: A forced breath out into a tube measures how much air the lungs can move and how fast. It is the test that diagnoses and grades asthma and COPD by separating airways that are narrowed (obstruction) from lungs that are stiff or small (restriction).

measures.meaning: The volume blown out in the first second; reduced when airways are narrowed.
Forced vital capacity, the total volume blown out; reduced when lungs are small or stiff.
Below 0.7 defines airflow obstruction (asthma, COPD).
FEV1 improving by 12% and 200 mL after a bronchodilator suggests asthma rather than COPD.
The fastest flow, measured at home on a hand-held meter to track asthma control.

whyOrdered: Breathlessness, wheeze or chronic cough
Smokers over 35 with symptoms (COPD screening)
Asthma diagnosis and monitoring
Before lung or major surgery
Occupational lung disease surveillance
spirometry.how: Take the deepest breath possible and blast it out as hard and long as possible through a mouthpiece, repeated three times; 15-30 minutes with a bronchodilator test.
spirometry.preparation: Avoid inhalers, big meals, alcohol and vigorous exercise before the test as instructed.

interpretation.meaning: COPD; severity graded by FEV1 as % predicted
Asthma
Restrictive pattern: fibrosis, chest wall or muscle disease, obesity; full lung function tests next

spirometry.limitations: Depends on effort and technique; normal spirometry between attacks does not exclude asthma. Not safe soon after a heart attack, eye surgery or pneumothorax.

pulmonary-function-tests.name: Full pulmonary function tests
pulmonary-function-tests.what: Spirometry plus measurements it cannot make: the total volume of the lungs including the air that cannot be blown out, and how easily gas crosses from the air sacs into blood (gas transfer, DLCO). Together they classify almost any lung disease.

measures.item: Total lung capacity and residual volume
measures.meaning: Measured in a sealed booth (plethysmography) or by gas dilution; high in emphysema (air trapping), low in fibrosis.
How much of a trace of carbon monoxide crosses into blood in one breath; reduced in emphysema, fibrosis and pulmonary vascular disease, raised in lung bleeding.
The shape reveals upper airway obstruction and the site of narrowing.
For suspected neuromuscular weakness.

whyOrdered: Unexplained breathlessness with normal spirometry
Interstitial lung disease and sarcoidosis
Assessing fitness for lung resection or chemotherapy (bleomycin)
Neuromuscular disease affecting breathing
Grading emphysema
pulmonary-function-tests.how: Sitting in a clear booth breathing through a mouthpiece with a nose clip through a series of manoeuvres, about an hour.
pulmonary-function-tests.preparation: As for spirometry; avoid smoking for 24 hours because carbon monoxide affects gas transfer.

interpretation.finding: Obstruction with high residual volume and low DLCO
interpretation.meaning: Emphysema
Pulmonary fibrosis or other interstitial disease
Chest wall, obesity or muscle weakness rather than lung parenchyma
Pulmonary vascular disease, early fibrosis, anaemia

pulmonary-function-tests.limitations: Anaemia lowers DLCO; results are compared with predicted values that depend on age, sex, height and ethnicity.

pulse-oximetry.name: Pulse oximetry and blood gases
pulse-oximetry.what: A clip on the fingertip shines red and infrared light through the tissue and reads the colour of pulsing blood to estimate how saturated haemoglobin is with oxygen. When more precision or a carbon dioxide level is needed, an arterial blood gas takes blood directly from an artery.

measures.meaning: 95-100% normal in healthy adults; 88-92% is the target in people with COPD who retain carbon dioxide.
The pressure of dissolved oxygen; below 8 kPa on air defines respiratory failure.
High when ventilation is inadequate (type 2 respiratory failure); low with hyperventilation.
Acid-base status: respiratory or metabolic acidosis and alkalosis.
Rises when tissues are starved of oxygen; a key sepsis marker.

whyOrdered: Any breathless or unwell patient (oximetry is a vital sign)
Pneumonia, COVID-19, asthma attacks, COPD flares
Monitoring oxygen therapy and ventilation
Suspected sepsis, diabetic ketoacidosis, poisoning (blood gas)
Sleep apnoea screening overnight
pulse-oximetry.how: The probe reads within seconds; a blood gas needs a needle in the radial artery at the wrist, which stings briefly, with pressure afterwards.
pulse-oximetry.preparation: Warm hands and remove nail varnish for oximetry.

interpretation.meaning: Hypoxaemia; oxygen and urgent assessment
Acute type 2 respiratory failure; may need ventilatory support

interpretation.finding: Low pH, low bicarbonate, high lactate
interpretation.meaning: Metabolic acidosis from sepsis or poor perfusion

pulse-oximetry.limitations: Oximetry misreads with cold hands, poor circulation, nail varnish, movement, carbon monoxide poisoning and, to a degree, darker skin; it says nothing about carbon dioxide. A normal saturation does not mean breathing is adequate.

endoscopy.name: Endoscopy (as a test)
endoscopy.what: A flexible or rigid tube with a camera passed into a body cavity through a natural opening or a small cut, so the lining can be seen directly and sampled. Each region has its own scope: the gullet and stomach (gastroscopy), the large bowel (colonoscopy), the airways (bronchoscopy), the bladder (cystoscopy) and joints (arthroscopy).

measures.meaning: Inflammation, ulcers, bleeding, polyps and tumours are seen and photographed.
Tiny samples taken painlessly from the lining for microscopy.
Polyps removed, bleeding stopped, narrowings stretched, stones retrieved at the same sitting.

whyOrdered: Difficulty swallowing, persistent indigestion, vomiting blood, weight loss (gastroscopy)
Bleeding from the bowel, change in bowel habit, positive stool screening test, anaemia (colonoscopy)
Coughing blood, a shadow on a chest scan (bronchoscopy)
Blood in the urine (cystoscopy)
Surveillance of Barrett oesophagus, ulcerative colitis, polyps
endoscopy.how: Usually a day case with throat spray or sedation; 10-45 minutes depending on the scope. Full details are on each procedure page.
endoscopy.preparation: Fasting for upper scopes; bowel preparation laxatives for colonoscopy; stop blood thinners as instructed.

interpretation.meaning: High re-bleeding risk; treated endoscopically
Surveillance interval set by number and size
Staging scans and multidisciplinary team planning

endoscopy.limitations: Invasive with small risks of bleeding and perforation; the small bowel is mostly out of reach (capsule endoscopy covers it).

biopsy.name: Biopsy
biopsy.what: Removal of a small piece of tissue or a few cells so a pathologist can examine them under the microscope. It is the only way to prove most cancers and many inflammatory diseases, and it grades and types a tumour so that treatment can be planned.

measures.meaning: The architecture of the tissue: normal, inflamed, precancerous or malignant, and which type.
How abnormal the cells look, which predicts how aggressively a cancer behaves.
Protein and gene tests on the sample (HER2, EGFR, PD-L1) that decide targeted treatment.
For excision biopsies, whether abnormal tissue reaches the edge.

whyOrdered: A lump, mass or shadow on imaging
Abnormal cells on a screening test
Unexplained organ inflammation (liver, kidney, muscle, skin)
Staging lymph nodes
Monitoring transplant rejection
biopsy.how: Depends on the site: a needle through the skin guided by ultrasound or CT, forceps through an endoscope, a punch or shave of the skin, or surgical removal. Local anaesthetic for most; results in days to two weeks.
biopsy.preparation: Blood thinners may be paused; clotting checked for liver and kidney biopsies.

interpretation.meaning: No cancer; may still explain symptoms (inflammation, infection)
Precancerous change; treat or survey
Cancer confirmed; staged with imaging and discussed by a multidisciplinary team
Too little tissue; repeat

biopsy.limitations: Samples a tiny fraction of an organ and can miss a lesion; small bleeding and infection risks, higher for deep organs.

genetic-testing.name: Genetic testing
genetic-testing.what: Reading part or all of a person's DNA (from blood or saliva) or a tumour's DNA (from a biopsy) to find variants that cause disease, raise risk, or predict which drug will work. Modern sequencing panels test hundreds of genes at once.

measures.meaning: Confirms a suspected inherited condition (cystic fibrosis, Huntington disease, familial hypercholesterolaemia).
Finds high-risk variants before disease appears (BRCA1/2 for breast and ovarian cancer, Lynch syndrome for bowel cancer).
Mutations in the cancer itself (EGFR, ALK, KRAS in lung cancer) that match targeted drugs.
Variants that change how drugs are handled (DPYD before fluorouracil, HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir).

whyOrdered: A family history of cancer at young ages or in several relatives
A child with developmental problems or an unexplained syndrome
Choosing targeted cancer treatment
Planning a pregnancy in carriers of recessive conditions
Sudden cardiac death in a young relative
genetic-testing.how: A blood or saliva sample after genetic counselling; results take weeks. Tumour testing uses the existing biopsy.
genetic-testing.preparation: Counselling before predictive tests, because results affect relatives and insurance in some countries.

interpretation.meaning: Diagnosis confirmed or high risk established; cascade testing offered to relatives
Cannot be interpreted yet; not used for clinical decisions
Lowers but does not abolish risk; the test only reads the genes on the panel

genetic-testing.limitations: Most common diseases are polygenic and environmental, so a single gene test says little; incidental findings and implications for family members need careful counselling.

microbiology-tests.name: Microbiology tests
microbiology-tests.what: Tests that find the organism causing an infection: growing it on culture, detecting its genes by PCR, its proteins by antigen tests, or the antibodies the body makes against it. Culture also reports which antibiotics work.

measures.meaning: Two bottles from separate sites before antibiotics; growth within 48 hours confirms bloodstream infection and its organism.
Throat, wound, genital and sputum samples cultured or tested by PCR.
Fast detection of viruses (COVID-19, influenza) and hard-to-grow bacteria.
Antibodies show past or current infection (hepatitis, HIV, glandular fever) and immunity after vaccination.
Bacteria, parasites and C. difficile toxin; faecal immunochemical test screens for bowel cancer.

whyOrdered: Fever with no obvious source, rigors, suspected sepsis
Pneumonia, urinary infection, wound infection, meningitis
Diarrhoea lasting more than a few days or after travel
Screening for HIV, hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections
Outbreak control and infection prevention (MRSA screening)
microbiology-tests.how: Samples taken with sterile technique, ideally before antibiotics; results from hours (PCR) to days (culture) or weeks (TB).
microbiology-tests.preparation: None for most; clean-catch technique for urine, deep cough for sputum.

interpretation.finding: Two blood cultures grow the same organism
interpretation.meaning: True bacteraemia; find the source and treat for the right duration

interpretation.finding: Skin organism in one bottle only
interpretation.meaning: Probably contamination
Antiviral treatment if early and at risk; isolation
Antibiotic changed to a sensitive agent; infection control alerted

microbiology-tests.limitations: Cultures are negative in a third of sepsis cases, especially after antibiotics; a positive result can mean colonisation rather than infection.

troponin.name: Troponin test
troponin.what: A blood test for cardiac troponin, a protein released when heart muscle cells are injured. It is the test that rules a heart attack in or out: with modern high-sensitivity assays, a value above the assay's upper limit and a rise or fall between two samples taken a few hours apart, read alongside the symptoms and the ECG, defines acute myocardial injury.

measures.meaning: Starts rising 1-3 hours after heart muscle injury, peaks at about 24 hours and can stay raised for one to two weeks. A change between serial samples separates an acute event from a stable, chronically raised level.

whyOrdered: Chest pain or other symptoms of a possible heart attack (on arrival and again after 1-3 hours)
Suspected myocarditis or pericarditis
Assessing heart injury in pulmonary embolism, sepsis and critical illness
After cardiac procedures, to detect procedure-related injury
Risk stratification in acute coronary syndromes
troponin.how: A venous blood sample; a second sample is timed from symptom onset or from arrival so that a rise or fall can be seen. Results are usually available within an hour in emergency departments.

interpretation.finding: Troponin above the assay's 99th percentile with a rise or fall between samples
interpretation.meaning: Acute myocardial injury; with symptoms of ischaemia, ECG change or imaging evidence it is classified as a myocardial infarction

interpretation.finding: Chronically raised, flat troponin on repeat samples
interpretation.meaning: Injury without an acute event: chronic kidney disease, heart failure, structural heart disease, older age

interpretation.finding: Very low or undetectable troponin hours after symptom onset
interpretation.meaning: Acute infarction is very unlikely; other causes of the symptoms are considered

interpretation.finding: Raised troponin with a clear non-cardiac illness
interpretation.meaning: Pulmonary embolism, sepsis, kidney failure, a very fast rhythm or extreme exertion can all release troponin

troponin.limitations: Troponin says that heart muscle was injured, not why: many conditions other than a blocked coronary artery raise it. A single sample taken too early can be normal, so the timing of the second sample matters. Each assay has its own reference limit, and results from different hospitals are not directly comparable.
troponin.resultType: Numeric, compared with the assay's 99th-percentile upper reference limit and with the previous sample

quick.sample: Blood from a vein, two samples a few hours apart
quick.usedFor: Suspected heart attack, heart muscle injury
quick.measures: Cardiac troponin I or T released from injured heart muscle

components.name: High-sensitivity troponin
components.measures: Cardiac troponin I or T in blood
components.high: Acute injury (rise or fall pattern) or chronic injury (stable level): infarction, myocarditis, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, kidney disease
components.low: A low level is expected; it makes acute infarction unlikely when the timing is right

troponin.rangeNote: There is no 'normal range' in the usual sense: each assay has its own 99th-percentile upper reference limit, often different for women and men, and the diagnosis rests on a change between samples rather than on a single number.

thresholds.name: Myocardial injury
thresholds.value: above the assay's 99th percentile upper reference limit
thresholds.context: Acute injury requires a rise and/or fall on serial samples; with evidence of ischaemia it is a myocardial infarction

factors: Time since symptom onset: sampling too early can miss the rise
Kidney function, which slows clearance
The assay used and its sex-specific limits
Very rarely, interfering antibodies in the sample
Recent strenuous exercise, cardioversion or cardiac procedures
cannotTell: Whether the injury was caused by a blocked coronary artery or by something else
Whether the heart's pumping function is reduced (that needs an echocardiogram)
Whether chest pain that started minutes ago is a heart attack, until the second sample
troponin.medicinesNote: Few medicines change troponin directly; cardiotoxic chemotherapy and some drugs that cause myocarditis can raise it.

bnp.name: BNP and NT-proBNP test
bnp.what: A blood test for the natriuretic peptides the heart's ventricles release when they are stretched by high pressure or extra volume. It is the first test for suspected heart failure: a normal level makes heart failure unlikely, while a raised level in a breathless person calls for an echocardiogram and specialist assessment within a set time.

measures.meaning: Laboratories measure one or the other; they are not interchangeable and have separate thresholds. Both rise with ventricular wall stress from heart failure, valve disease, atrial fibrillation and pulmonary embolism.

whyOrdered: Breathlessness, ankle swelling or fatigue where heart failure is possible
Deciding how urgently a person needs echocardiography
Prognosis and monitoring of known heart failure
Assessing the heart in pulmonary embolism and sepsis
bnp.how: A venous blood sample; no special timing.

interpretation.finding: NT-proBNP below 400 ng/L (or BNP below 100 ng/L) in an untreated person
interpretation.meaning: Heart failure is unlikely; another cause of the symptoms is looked for
Heart failure possible: referral for echocardiography and specialist assessment within six weeks in UK guidance
High likelihood and worse prognosis: urgent referral within two weeks

interpretation.finding: Raised level with obesity or on heart-failure treatment
interpretation.meaning: Obesity lowers natriuretic peptides and treatment changes them, so results are read with these in mind

bnp.limitations: Natriuretic peptides show that the heart is under strain, not why: kidney disease, older age, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism and sepsis all raise them, and obesity can lower them enough to mask heart failure. The test cannot describe the structure or pumping function of the heart; that is the echocardiogram's job.

bnp.resultType: Numeric, read against guideline referral thresholds

quick.usedFor: Suspected heart failure, monitoring heart failure
quick.measures: BNP or NT-proBNP released by stretched ventricles

components.measures: Natriuretic peptide concentration
components.high: Heart failure, valve disease, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism, kidney disease, older age
components.low: Obesity can lower the level; a low level makes heart failure unlikely

bnp.rangeNote: Instead of a laboratory reference interval, natriuretic peptides are read against guideline thresholds that decide how urgently a person is referred for echocardiography. The thresholds for BNP and NT-proBNP differ.
