Kidney function
Atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, lung disease
Heart-failure medicines, including diuretics and sacubitril/valsartan, which raises BNP but not NT-proBNP
cannotTell: Whether the heart's pumping is reduced or preserved
Which valve or chamber is affected
Whether breathlessness has a lung rather than a heart cause
bnp.medicinesNote: Sacubitril/valsartan raises BNP (which it stops being broken down) but not NT-proBNP; diuretics and other heart-failure treatment lower both.

crp.name: CRP test
crp.what: A blood test for C-reactive protein, a protein the liver releases within hours of significant inflammation, infection or tissue injury. It measures the size and course of an inflammatory response and how it changes with treatment, but not its cause.

measures.meaning: Rises within about 6 hours of a trigger, peaks at about 48 hours and falls quickly once the trigger resolves. Levels in the hundreds suggest bacterial infection or major inflammation; mild elevations are common and non-specific.

whyOrdered: Suspected infection or sepsis, and monitoring the response to antibiotics
Distinguishing inflammatory joint disease from wear-and-tear pain
Unexplained fever, weight loss or fatigue
Monitoring rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, polymyalgia and vasculitis
After surgery, where a rising level can signal a complication
crp.how: A venous blood sample; point-of-care fingerprick CRP is used in some primary-care settings to guide antibiotic decisions.

interpretation.meaning: Significant bacterial infection or major inflammation until proven otherwise
Minor inflammation, viral illness, obesity, smoking or recent exertion; interpreted with the clinical picture

interpretation.finding: Normal CRP with a high ESR
interpretation.meaning: Consider conditions that raise ESR without much CRP: myeloma, lupus, anaemia, pregnancy
The inflammation is settling; a persistently rising value after surgery prompts a search for infection or a leak

crp.limitations: Non-specific: it cannot say where the inflammation is or what is causing it. A normal CRP early in an illness does not exclude infection, and some infections (viral, some fungal) and lupus flares barely raise it. Steroids and immunosuppressants blunt the rise.
crp.specimen: Venous blood (serum or plasma); fingerprick for point-of-care tests
crp.resultType: Numeric; a laboratory reference interval, usually with an upper limit only

quick.measures: C-reactive protein, an acute-phase protein made by the liver

components.name: C-reactive protein
components.measures: Acute-phase protein concentration in blood
components.high: Bacterial infection, sepsis, surgery, trauma, inflammatory arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, cancer, mild elevation with obesity and smoking

crp.rangeNote: Laboratories report an upper reference limit for CRP that differs between methods; high-sensitivity assays used for cardiovascular risk have their own bands. There is no diagnostic threshold: a raised CRP is a prompt to look for the cause, not a diagnosis.
factors: Time since the illness began (the first hours can be normal)
Corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants blunt the rise
Obesity, smoking, pregnancy and oestrogens raise the baseline
Strenuous exercise in the previous day
cannotTell: Where the inflammation is or what is causing it
Whether an infection is bacterial or viral with certainty
Whether a person with a normal CRP has no serious illness
crp.medicinesNote: Corticosteroids, biologic anti-inflammatory drugs (particularly IL-6 inhibitors) and other immunosuppressants can keep CRP low despite active infection.

esr.name: ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate)
esr.what: An old but still useful test that measures how far red blood cells settle in a narrow tube in one hour. Inflammatory proteins such as fibrinogen and immunoglobulins make red cells stack and sink faster, so the ESR rises with inflammation, infection and some blood disorders, more slowly and less specifically than CRP.

measures.meaning: The distance in millimetres the red cells fall in an hour. Rises over days with inflammation and falls over weeks after it resolves; also raised by anaemia, pregnancy, older age and high immunoglobulin levels.

whyOrdered: Suspected temporal (giant cell) arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica, where it is part of the diagnostic picture
Monitoring rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and other long-term inflammatory diseases
Suspected myeloma and other conditions that raise immunoglobulins
Unexplained symptoms where inflammation is one possibility, alongside CRP
esr.how: A venous blood sample in an anticoagulant tube, tested within a few hours.

interpretation.meaning: Giant cell arteritis, myeloma, serious infection or widespread cancer are among the causes considered
Active inflammation or infection
Anaemia, pregnancy, kidney disease, lupus, myeloma or simply older age
Makes active inflammatory disease less likely but does not exclude it; the ESR is slow to rise

esr.limitations: The ESR is influenced by many things other than inflammation, including anaemia, red-cell shape, pregnancy, age and immunoglobulin levels, and it changes slowly. CRP is preferred for tracking acute infection; the ESR keeps a place in a few conditions and in long-term monitoring.
esr.specimen: Venous blood in an EDTA or citrate tube
esr.resultType: Numeric (mm/h); reference limit rises with age

quick.usedFor: Inflammatory disease, giant cell arteritis, myeloma, monitoring
quick.measures: How quickly red cells settle, a proxy for inflammatory proteins

components.name: Sedimentation rate
components.measures: Red-cell settling distance in one hour
components.high: Inflammation, infection, anaemia, pregnancy, myeloma, older age, kidney disease
components.low: Polycythaemia, sickle cell disease, very high white-cell counts (low or falsely low)

esr.rangeNote: Reference limits depend on age and sex and rise in older adults; laboratories publish their own. No ESR value diagnoses a disease on its own.
factors: Anaemia and red-cell shape (sickle cells settle slowly)
Pregnancy, age and sex
Time between sampling and testing
High immunoglobulin or fibrinogen levels from any cause
cannotTell: What is causing the inflammation
How recently the inflammation began (it lags by days)
Whether a normal result excludes disease
esr.medicinesNote: Corticosteroids and anti-inflammatory biologics lower it; oral contraceptives and some intravenous immunoglobulin preparations raise it.

tsh.name: TSH test
tsh.what: The single most sensitive blood test of thyroid function: TSH from the pituitary rises when the thyroid is underactive and falls when it is overactive, often before the thyroid hormones themselves leave their reference range. It is the first-line screening test and the value used to adjust levothyroxine.

measures.meaning: The pituitary's signal to the thyroid. High TSH means the pituitary is pushing a failing thyroid (hypothyroidism); very low TSH means it is being suppressed by excess thyroid hormone (hyperthyroidism). Laboratories add free T4 automatically when TSH is abnormal.

whyOrdered: Tiredness, weight change, feeling cold or hot, palpitations, anxiety, constipation or low mood
A goitre, neck lump or family history of thyroid disease
Atrial fibrillation, high cholesterol, depression, infertility or menstrual change
Monitoring levothyroxine (6-8 weeks after a dose change, then yearly) or antithyroid drugs
Before and during pregnancy in women with thyroid disease; on amiodarone or lithium
tsh.how: A venous blood sample at any time of day; people on levothyroxine usually take the dose after the sample.
tsh.preparation: None; tell the laboratory about biotin supplements, which can interfere with the assay and are paused for two days before the test.

interpretation.finding: High TSH with low free T4
interpretation.meaning: Primary hypothyroidism (the thyroid itself is failing)

interpretation.finding: High TSH with normal free T4
interpretation.meaning: Subclinical hypothyroidism: often repeated after three months; treatment considered if TSH stays above 10 mU/L or with symptoms, pregnancy or planning pregnancy

interpretation.finding: Low TSH with high free T4 or T3
interpretation.meaning: Hyperthyroidism: Graves disease, toxic nodules or thyroiditis

interpretation.finding: Low TSH with low free T4
interpretation.meaning: Pituitary (secondary) hypothyroidism, severe non-thyroidal illness or recent over-treatment; TSH alone cannot be trusted here

tsh.limitations: TSH is unreliable when the pituitary is diseased, during and shortly after severe illness ('sick euthyroid'), in the first trimester of pregnancy and with some medicines; it takes about six weeks to settle after a levothyroxine dose change, so testing sooner misleads. A normal TSH does not exclude thyroid problems that involve antibodies or nodules.

components.name: TSH
components.measures: Pituitary thyroid-stimulating hormone
components.high: Hypothyroidism, under-replacement with levothyroxine, recovery from illness
components.low: Hyperthyroidism, over-replacement, pituitary disease, first-trimester pregnancy

components.name: Free T4 (added when TSH is abnormal)
components.measures: Unbound thyroxine
components.high: Hyperthyroidism, excess levothyroxine

thresholds.name: Subclinical hypothyroidism: consider levothyroxine
thresholds.value: TSH 10 or above on two occasions three months apart
thresholds.context: Adults with raised TSH and normal free T4; below 10 mU/L treatment depends on symptoms and circumstances

Biotin supplements and some antibodies interfere with immunoassays
Levothyroxine timing, adherence and absorption (iron, calcium, proton pump inhibitors reduce absorption)
Pregnancy, older age, amiodarone, lithium, high-dose steroids and dopamine
cannotTell: The cause of an over- or underactive thyroid (antibodies, scans or ultrasound are needed)
Thyroid status when the pituitary itself is diseased
Whether a nodule or goitre is present
tsh.medicinesNote: Levothyroxine and antithyroid drugs are the intended influences; amiodarone, lithium, interferon and immune checkpoint inhibitors can cause thyroid dysfunction; biotin interferes with the assay itself.

ferritin.name: Ferritin test
ferritin.what: A blood test that estimates the body's iron stores by measuring ferritin, the protein that holds iron inside cells. It is the best single test for iron deficiency, the commonest cause of anaemia, and it also detects iron overload; because ferritin rises with inflammation, it is often read alongside CRP.

measures.meaning: Mirrors stored iron: low when stores are exhausted, high with iron overload but also with inflammation, infection, liver disease, alcohol and cancer.

whyOrdered: Anaemia, especially with small red cells (low MCV)
Tiredness, restless legs, hair loss or brittle nails where iron deficiency is suspected
Heavy periods, pregnancy, vegetarian or vegan diets, coeliac disease, after gastric surgery
Suspected haemochromatosis or iron overload from repeated transfusions
Monitoring iron treatment and, in chronic kidney disease and heart failure, iron status before intravenous iron
ferritin.how: A venous blood sample, often with a full blood count and sometimes transferrin saturation.
ferritin.preparation: None; a recent iron infusion or blood transfusion should be mentioned.

interpretation.finding: Ferritin below about 30 µg/L in an adult
interpretation.meaning: Iron stores are depleted (iron deficiency), whether or not anaemia is present yet; the cause, often blood loss, is then looked for

interpretation.finding: Normal ferritin with raised CRP and anaemia
interpretation.meaning: Inflammation may be masking iron deficiency; transferrin saturation or a trial of iron helps decide
Iron overload (haemochromatosis, transfusions) or severe inflammation, liver disease, cancer or a haemophagocytic syndrome
Stores are being replenished; treatment usually continues for months after haemoglobin normalises

ferritin.limitations: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein: any inflammation, infection, liver disease or alcohol excess raises it and can hide a deficiency. It does not show why iron is low; in adults iron deficiency is a reason to look for a source of blood loss, particularly in the gut.
ferritin.resultType: Numeric with a laboratory reference interval; a guideline cut-off defines depleted stores

quick.measures: Ferritin, the iron-storage protein, as a proxy for body iron stores

components.name: Serum ferritin
components.measures: Iron-storage protein in blood
components.high: Inflammation, infection, liver disease, alcohol, iron overload, cancer
components.low: Iron deficiency from blood loss, poor intake, malabsorption or pregnancy

ferritin.rangeNote: Laboratories publish reference intervals that differ by sex and age, but the clinical question 'are iron stores depleted?' is answered with a guideline cut-off rather than the lower reference limit, and the cut-off is raised when inflammation is present.

thresholds.name: Iron deficiency
thresholds.context: Adults; ferritin below this level confirms depleted iron stores. With coexisting inflammation a higher cut-off is used

factors: Inflammation and infection raise ferritin regardless of iron stores
Liver disease, alcohol, obesity and metabolic syndrome
Recent iron infusion or transfusion
Time of day and assay differences between laboratories
cannotTell: Why iron is low (the source of blood loss must be sought separately)
Iron status reliably during active inflammation without other tests
Whether anaemia is due to something other than iron, such as B12 or folate deficiency
ferritin.medicinesNote: Oral and intravenous iron raise it; regular aspirin or NSAID use can cause the gut blood loss that lowers it; proton pump inhibitors reduce iron absorption.

creatinine-egfr.name: Creatinine and eGFR
creatinine-egfr.what: The everyday measure of how well the kidneys filter. Creatinine, a waste product of muscle, builds up in blood as filtration falls; the laboratory converts it, with age and sex, into an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), the number used to stage chronic kidney disease, detect acute kidney injury and adjust the doses of many medicines.

measures.meaning: Produced steadily by muscle and cleared by the glomeruli; rises when filtration falls, but only after a substantial loss of function
Millilitres of blood filtered per minute, estimated from creatinine by the CKD-EPI equation and adjusted to a standard body size; below 60 for three months defines chronic kidney disease

whyOrdered: Screening people with diabetes, high blood pressure or cardiovascular disease
Before starting or adjusting medicines cleared by the kidney (metformin, DOACs, many antibiotics) and before contrast scans
Swelling, reduced urine, tiredness, nausea or confusion
Acute illness, dehydration, vomiting or diarrhoea, particularly in people on ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics or NSAIDs
Monitoring chronic kidney disease, lithium and nephrotoxic drugs
creatinine-egfr.how: A venous blood sample; usually reported together with urea and electrolytes, and paired with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio when kidney disease is being assessed.
creatinine-egfr.preparation: None; avoid a large meat meal and strenuous exercise the day before if the result matters for staging, and mention creatine supplements.

interpretation.finding: Creatinine rising over hours to days
interpretation.meaning: Acute kidney injury: dehydration, sepsis, obstruction or drugs; the eGFR is unreliable while the value is changing

interpretation.finding: eGFR below 60 on two tests at least 90 days apart
interpretation.meaning: Chronic kidney disease, staged G3a to G5 by the value and combined with the urine albumin category

interpretation.finding: eGFR 60-89 with no markers of kidney damage
interpretation.meaning: Not chronic kidney disease on its own; common with age

interpretation.finding: Small creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
interpretation.meaning: Expected; a rise above about 30% prompts review of the dose and a search for renal artery narrowing

creatinine-egfr.limitations: Creatinine depends on muscle mass, so eGFR overestimates function in frail people and underestimates it in the very muscular; the equation assumes a steady state and is inaccurate in pregnancy, at extremes of body size and in rapidly changing illness. About half of kidney function can be lost before creatinine leaves the reference interval. Cystatin C offers a second estimate when the creatinine-based one is doubtful.

Cooked meat within the previous 12 hours and strenuous exercise
Hydration and acute illness (the estimate assumes a steady state)

Pregnancy, where filtration normally increases
cannotTell: The cause of kidney disease (that needs urine tests, imaging and sometimes a biopsy)
Whether protein is leaking into the urine (the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio does that)
Kidney function precisely near the normal range, where a cystatin C estimate can confirm the finding
creatinine-egfr.medicinesNote: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, lithium, some antibiotics and contrast media can reduce filtration; trimethoprim raises creatinine by blocking its secretion without changing true function; metformin, DOACs and many antibiotics are dosed by eGFR.
